title: How Scientific Revolutions Happen
description: Four extracts from a public talk and discussion about how science changes: paradigms, anomalies, a famous case and a critique.
instructions: Read the questions for each part first. Then press Play and listen. Choose the best answer for each question.

parts.title: Part 1 · A public talk
parts.intro: You will hear a historian of science beginning a public talk.

script.speaker: Dr Whitfield
script.text: Most of us were taught that science advances like a staircase, with each generation adding a step to the one before. It is a comforting picture, but about sixty years ago a historian of science published a short book arguing that it is largely wrong. His claim was that science alternates between long, quiet periods and short, turbulent ones, and that the second kind is not an extension of the first but a break from it.

script.speaker: Dr Whitfield
script.text: The quiet periods he called normal science. During them, researchers share a framework, a set of assumptions about what the world is like, which questions are worth asking and what counts as a good answer. He called that framework a paradigm. Within it, the work resembles solving jigsaw puzzles. The picture on the box is already known, and the scientist's job is to fit the pieces.

script.speaker: Dr Whitfield
script.text: Now, what happens when a piece will not fit? Usually, nothing very dramatic. The researcher assumes that the equipment was faulty, or that she made an error, and sets the result aside. This is not stubbornness. A framework that dropped at every awkward measurement would be useless, and in most cases the anomaly really is a mistake.

script.speaker: Dr Whitfield
script.text: But sometimes anomalies accumulate. They begin to cluster around the same point, and they resist every attempt to explain them away. A sense of unease spreads through the field, and a few young or unconventional researchers start to explore alternatives. That, in his account, is the beginning of a crisis.

script.speaker: Dr Whitfield
script.text: I want to stress something that is often overlooked. The new framework does not win simply because it is more accurate. The rival schools often disagree about what the evidence even is, so they can talk past one another. Persuasion, generations and even personality play a part. That is what made the book so controversial, because it suggested that science, however rational, is also a human enterprise.

parts.title: Part 2 · Questions after the talk
parts.intro: You will hear a lecturer, Dr Chen, answering a question from a student, Nam.

script.speaker: Nam
script.text: Dr Chen, I'm a bit unsettled by this. If a new paradigm wins partly through persuasion, doesn't that mean science is no more objective than, say, fashion?

script.speaker: Dr Chen
script.text: That is the reading that alarmed many people, and it is a misreading, or at least an exaggeration. The author himself insisted that the new framework usually solves more problems than the old one and does so more precisely. Nobody switched back to the old astronomy because the new one was merely fashionable.

script.speaker: Nam
script.text: But if two paradigms define the evidence differently, how can we compare them at all?

script.speaker: Dr Chen
script.text: Imperfectly, but not impossibly. Scientists can still ask which framework predicts more accurately, which is simpler and which opens up fruitful lines of research. Those criteria are not mechanical rules, and reasonable people may weigh them differently. That's why a transition takes time instead of happening overnight.

script.speaker: Nam
script.text: So the criticism is half right.

script.speaker: Dr Chen
script.text: I would put it differently. The book showed that scientific judgement involves more than logic, but it never showed that judgement is arbitrary. A good doctor also uses judgement, and we do not conclude that medicine is a matter of taste.

script.speaker: Nam
script.text: Then what would you say is the main lesson?

script.speaker: Dr Chen
script.text: Humility, I think. The framework you take for granted may one day look as odd as the ones we now find quaint. And, practically, that we should treat unusual results with curiosity rather than contempt, because the next revolution will begin as somebody's inconvenient anomaly.

script.speaker: Nam
script.text: That's quite a sobering thought for a student about to start a dissertation.

script.speaker: Dr Chen
script.text: Or an encouraging one. Somebody must find the anomalies, after all.

parts.title: Part 3 · A case study
parts.intro: You will hear a geologist, Dr Santos, describing how an idea about continents was accepted.

script.speaker: Dr Santos
script.text: My favourite example is the idea that continents move. In the early twentieth century, a German meteorologist proposed that the continents had once formed a single landmass and had since drifted apart. His evidence was impressive. The coastlines of South America and Africa fit like pieces of a puzzle, and identical fossils turn up on opposite sides of the ocean.

script.speaker: Dr Santos
script.text: Yet geologists rejected it for decades. The proposer was an outsider, not a geologist, which counted against him. More importantly, he could not explain how continents could plough through the solid ocean floor. Without a mechanism, the evidence looked like a series of coincidences, and many experts treated it as fantasy.

script.speaker: Dr Santos
script.text: Then, in the nineteen fifties and sixties, new instruments transformed the field. Surveys of the sea floor revealed a vast chain of underwater mountains with new rock emerging along its centre, and patterns of magnetism in that rock were symmetrical on either side. Suddenly, the ocean floor looked like a conveyor belt, and continents could ride on it rather than ploughing through it.

script.speaker: Dr Santos
script.text: Notice the sequence. The anomalies had been available for fifty years, but it took a new mechanism, and a new generation of researchers, to make them persuasive. Some senior figures never changed their minds. The idea won, as one physicist said, not because opponents were convinced but because they eventually retired.

script.speaker: Dr Santos
script.text: I find the story both humbling and reassuring. It shows how stubborn a field can be, but also how decisive evidence eventually becomes. Within a decade, the textbooks had been rewritten, and students now find it hard to believe there was ever a controversy.

parts.title: Part 4 · A closing discussion
parts.intro: You will hear a presenter, Linh, and a philosopher, Dr Brennan, discussing whether revolutions still happen.

script.speaker: Linh
script.text: Dr Brennan, we hear the word revolution constantly now, in medicine, in computing and in biology. Is science really still being overturned?

script.speaker: Dr Brennan
script.text: I'd be sceptical of the word. Real overturning is rare. Most of what's called a revolution today is a powerful new tool, such as gene editing or machine learning, which accelerates work within existing frameworks. That can be transformative without being revolutionary in the strict sense.

script.speaker: Linh
script.text: So the hype is a little inflated.

script.speaker: Dr Brennan
script.text: Often. Although I wouldn't want to be complacent. Some fields are, I think, in a state of unresolved tension. Physicists still cannot reconcile their two greatest theories, and neuroscientists still have no agreed account of how the brain produces experience. Those might be the anomalies that ripen into something larger.

script.speaker: Linh
script.text: How would we even know we were in the middle of one?

script.speaker: Dr Brennan
script.text: We wouldn't, most likely. Revolutions look obvious only in retrospect. Those living through the change seldom call it that. They simply find that old questions have stopped making sense and new ones have taken their place.

script.speaker: Linh
script.text: Does that make you pessimistic?

script.speaker: Dr Brennan
script.text: Quite the contrary. It makes me hopeful that science remains capable of surprising itself. A discipline that could never be overturned would be a creed, not a science. The willingness to be wrong, I would argue, is the most valuable thing it has.

questions.text: What was the historian's central claim about science?
options: It is mainly driven by changing fashion in society
It is simply a long series of avoidable mistakes by researchers
It advances smoothly, like a staircase, over time
It alternates between quiet periods and abrupt breaks
questions.explanation: He argued that science alternates between long quiet periods and short turbulent ones, which are a break.

evidence.quote: science alternates between long, quiet periods and short, turbulent ones

questions.text: What did he call the shared framework in normal science?
options: An anomaly
A paradigm
A theory
A puzzle
questions.explanation: He called the framework a paradigm.

evidence.quote: He called that framework a paradigm.

questions.text: Why do researchers usually set aside an anomalous result?
options: They are paid by their institutions to ignore them
They are afraid of upsetting their senior colleagues
A framework dropped at every anomaly would be useless
They never notice errors in their own equipment
questions.explanation: The speaker says it is not stubbornness since a framework dropped at every awkward measurement would be useless.

evidence.quote: A framework that dropped at every awkward measurement would be useless

questions.text: What marks the beginning of a crisis?
options: A new and more precise instrument is bought
Anomalies accumulate and resist explanation
A senior professor retires from the field
A single serious mistake is found in a result
questions.explanation: Anomalies cluster and resist every attempt to explain them away.

evidence.quote: they resist every attempt to explain them away

questions.text: What does he stress about why a new framework wins?
options: Money from funding bodies decides the outcome
The age of researchers is irrelevant to it
Accuracy alone does not decide the outcome
Accuracy is the only factor that matters
questions.explanation: He says it does not win simply because it is more accurate; persuasion and generations play a part.

evidence.quote: does not win simply because it is more accurate

questions.text: Why is Nam unsettled by the talk?
options: He wants to see more evidence for the argument
He disagrees with the dates the lecturer gave
He thinks the historian was dishonest about his sources
He fears science may be no more objective than fashion
questions.explanation: He asks whether persuasion makes science no more objective than fashion.

evidence.quote: doesn't that mean science is no more objective than, say, fashion?

questions.text: How does Dr Chen respond to the fashion idea?
options: She calls it an exaggeration
She ignores it
She says it is a recent theory
She agrees entirely
questions.explanation: She calls it a misreading, or at least an exaggeration.

evidence.quote: it is a misreading, or at least an exaggeration

questions.text: Why does Dr Chen mention a doctor?
options: To describe a case study from her own practice
To explain how doctors are trained to use evidence
To suggest that medicine is not truly scientific
To show that judgement is not the same as arbitrariness
questions.explanation: She says a good doctor uses judgement but medicine is not a matter of taste.

evidence.quote: we do not conclude that medicine is a matter of taste

questions.text: What main lesson does Dr Chen draw?
options: Always follow the majority view in a field
Humility and curiosity about unusual results
Never trust anomalies when they appear in your own results
Avoid new theories until they are proven
questions.explanation: She says the main lesson is humility and treating unusual results with curiosity.

evidence.quote: Humility, I think.

questions.text: How does Dr Chen respond to Nam's remark about his dissertation?
options: She changes the subject to something lighter
She tells him to be extremely careful
She apologises for upsetting him
She suggests it could be encouraging
questions.explanation: She says it could be an encouraging thought, since somebody must find anomalies.

evidence.quote: Or an encouraging one.

questions.text: What evidence supported the idea that continents move?
options: Earthquakes that damaged cities near the coast
Matching coastlines and fossils on either side of the ocean
The writings of ancient geologists on the subject
Studies of the weather over several continents
questions.explanation: Coastlines fit and identical fossils turn up on both sides of the ocean.

evidence.quote: identical fossils turn up on opposite sides of the ocean

questions.text: Why did geologists reject the idea for decades?
options: No mechanism explained how continents could move
Nobody in the field had bothered to read the original proposal
The evidence of matching coasts was missing
The fossils had been proved to be forged
questions.explanation: He could not explain how continents could plough through the ocean floor.

evidence.quote: he could not explain how continents could plough through the solid ocean floor

questions.text: What did sea floor surveys reveal?
options: Underwater mountains with new rock along their centre
Ancient cities lying on the ocean floor beneath the water
Large deposits of oil beneath the sea bed
A hidden continent beneath the Atlantic
questions.explanation: They revealed an underwater chain of mountains with new rock emerging along its centre.

evidence.quote: a vast chain of underwater mountains

questions.text: What does the quoted physicist suggest?
options: Opponents were quickly convinced by the evidence
Physicists have always disliked the study of geology
Opponents often fade away rather than change their minds
Evidence is much less important than most people think
questions.explanation: The idea won because opponents eventually retired.

evidence.quote: not because opponents were convinced but because they eventually retired

questions.text: Why does Dr Santos call the story humbling and reassuring?
options: It proves that she was right all along
It shows both stubbornness and the power of evidence
It shows how rich successful geologists became
It shows how fast textbooks can be written
questions.explanation: She says it shows how stubborn a field can be but also how decisive evidence eventually becomes.

evidence.quote: how stubborn a field can be, but also how decisive evidence eventually becomes

questions.text: What is Dr Brennan's attitude to calling modern advances revolutions?
options: He is sceptical
He is angry
He is indifferent
He is enthusiastic
questions.explanation: He says he would be sceptical of the word.

evidence.quote: I'd be sceptical of the word.

questions.text: What does he give as examples of unresolved tension?
options: Gene editing and machine learning in medicine
Reconciling two physics theories and explaining experience
Climate prediction and long-range weather forecasting
Computing and the foundations of mathematics
questions.explanation: He mentions physicists failing to reconcile their theories and neuroscience lacking an account of experience.

questions.text: Why will we probably not know if we are in a revolution?
options: Revolutions look obvious only in retrospect
They are always announced in advance by leading scientists
They never actually occur in modern times
Scientists hide them from the public
questions.explanation: He says revolutions look obvious only in retrospect.

evidence.quote: Revolutions look obvious only in retrospect.

questions.text: Why does he say the discussion makes him hopeful?
options: Scientists now agree on almost everything important
Science is still capable of surprising itself
Technology will soon replace theory
Science is nearly finished
questions.explanation: He says he is hopeful that science remains capable of surprising itself.

evidence.quote: science remains capable of surprising itself

questions.text: What point does he make by comparing science with a creed?
options: Willingness to be wrong is what makes it science
Science should reject belief of every kind, including creeds
Science is really a form of religion
Creeds are more reliable than theories
questions.explanation: A discipline that could never be overturned would be a creed; willingness to be wrong is valuable.

evidence.quote: A discipline that could never be overturned would be a creed, not a science.
